extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, journalism students, and policy analysts studying influences on news content
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess the institutional, economic, ownership, and governmental factors that shape news production and content (including prepackaged materials, owner/executive pressures, staff constraints, and medium-specific economic dynamics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prepackaged news (VNRs and print releases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political figures and government agencies frequently use prepackaged news such as VNRs and print releases to ensure the media carry desired messages; many such items are broadcast without stations acknowledging the government’s production role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether news segments are original reporting versus prepackaged material, whether the source/producer (e.g., government agency) is disclosed, and whether timing and distribution suggest strategic use (e.g., released near political events). Examples: Bush administration VNR on Medicare distributed in January 2004; studies finding hundreds of government-produced TV segments distributed 2001–2005.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of paid promotion and hidden government payments to commentators
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances where syndicated columnists or commentators were paid by government to promote policies without disclosing contracts (e.g., Armstrong Williams, Maggie Gallagher, Michael McManus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether opinion pieces, columns, or broadcasts that favor a policy disclose financial ties or contracts. Treat undisclosed payments as a serious ethical lapse; check syndication service responses and whether the column/service continued distribution after disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government/script review and covert placement in entertainment programming
rubrics_metrics.description: Government offices have reviewed scripts and arranged inclusion of subject matter in prime-time programming (e.g., ONDCP reviewed ~100 scripts across major networks), sometimes without networks making substantive changes but with the effect of advancing political messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine evidence of government script review or influence on entertainment content; consider whether networks disclosed such arrangements and whether subject-matter inclusion functioned as covert messaging (historical parallels: Nancy Reagan 'Just Say No' placements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic pressures / market-driven journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Media organizations operate within four markets—investors, advertisers, sources, and consumers—and market pressures, especially investors/owners, shape news production and priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the strength of investor/ advertiser/consumer pressures and their observable effects on content choices (e.g., prioritizing profit-generating stories). Use models that identify which markets exert most influence (McManus: investors most influential).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bottom-line pressure and perceived harm to news quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists increasingly report that emphasis on the bottom line is harming the quality of news coverage (surveys report large and growing percentages across print and broadcast journalists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use survey data or interviews to quantify perceptions of bottom-line pressure; track changes over time and differences by medium (e.g., 1999 vs. 2004 Pew findings; union surveys reporting high percentages). Consider this as an indicator of systemic economic constraints on quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner/executive pressure on story selection and handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners and top executives establish policy and can exert direct pressure on journalists about which stories to cover or how to treat them; management has legal/organizational incentives to serve owners' economic interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence of owner/executive requests (e.g., special handling of articles), reported instances where journalists felt pressured to report or not report stories, and organizational policies that reflect owners' priorities. Cite studies showing percentages of journalists reporting owner pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership concentration and content standardization/duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrated or chain ownership can lead to duplication of content across outlets, uniform editorial views, and reduced diversity of themes and frames (though findings across studies are mixed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare content diversity and duplication across independently owned and chain-owned outlets; check for standardized editorials, reused wire/chain copy, and reduced local distinctiveness. Note mixed empirical results (some studies find no duplication; others find standardization, e.g., Gannett comparisons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local vs. corporate ownership effects on local news time
rubrics_metrics.description: Locally owned television stations allocate more time to local news per half-hour newscast than nationally owned stations—ownership structure affects quantity of local coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure minutes of local news per newscast by ownership type. Use FCC and empirical studies (e.g., FCC study finding nearly six extra minutes for locally owned stations) as benchmarks; account for possible suppression or non-publication of internal studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership economic interests shaping editorial tone and issue coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners' potential to gain financially from policy outcomes correlates with more favorable coverage; outlets that stand to gain from a policy may give it favorable coverage or avoid coverage (e.g., Telecommunications Act studies, 'airwaves giveaway').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess editorial stance and hard-news framing relative to owners' financial stakes. Compare outlets with and without relevant holdings (e.g., newspapers with television holdings vs. those without) and analyze tone differences and frequency of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-specific sensitivity to economic pressures (broadcast greater than print)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast media (radio and TV) are hypothesized and evidenced to be more sensitive to profit pressures because nearly all income originates from advertising and programming decisions directly translate to commercial time trade-offs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating outlets, differentiate between broadcast and print economics: examine advertising dependency, program scheduling constraints, directness of competition, and survey findings showing higher perceived pressure among broadcast journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff size as a determinant of news quality and coverage breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: Larger news staffs and budgets are generally associated with higher-quality programming and greater capacity for local and hard news coverage; reductions in staff size are associated with perceived declines in quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use staff-size and budget metrics to predict quality and local coverage breadth; assess changes over time (e.g., cutbacks linked to coverage declines), and compare size to actual allocation of additional newscast time (risk of longer newscasts without proportional staff increases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Management and within-organization routines/constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Influences arising within the news organization include pressures from assignment editors and other superiors, journalist traits, and routine constraints such as time, staff, and resources that shape how journalists produce content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate newsroom routines, assignment processes, editorial hierarchies, and resource constraints to understand micro-level influences on content; consider both individual-level traits and organizational routines as joint determinants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda cutting and selective noncoverage to protect owner interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Media organizations that stand to benefit from certain policy issues may ignore or underreport those issues; conversely, outlets that do not stand to gain may provide more and more negative coverage (agenda cutting and omission as a form of influence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for systematic noncoverage or reduced prominence of issues that would advantage owners, and compare coverage frequency and tone across outlets. Use case studies (e.g., digital spectrum 'giveaway' coverage differences) to identify agenda-cutting patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradictory findings: corporate characteristics can also correlate with product quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Some studies find that newspapers with more corporate characteristics placed greater emphasis on product quality, complicating simple assumptions that corporate ownership always reduces quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ownership–quality relationships empirically and avoid blanket assumptions; include measures of product quality alongside ownership metrics and consider context-dependent effects reported in the literature (e.g., Demers' findings).
